source.title: Gradient-Energy Guided Block-Wise Perturbations for Sharpness-Aware Minimization
source.authors: Zheng-Hao Huang; Jia-Xin Deng; Jun-Biao Pang

record.tranche_reason: The study measures sharpness-related quantities and test accuracy while comparing SAM with a block-wise variant, but does not test the listed natural-versus-random-label generalization claims or the listed sharpness measure. Its results refine the interpretation of SAM allocation and report a mixed result for dominant Hessian statistics.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-accuracy comparisons and Hessian measurements for SAM and GEAR-SAM, plus allocation-share figures. Results cited from prior work are not rows. The paper does not compare training and test error gaps or study random-label memorization. Hessian eigenvalues and allocation shares are related measures, but do not test V7’s magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance.
record.test_reason: The study uses the sharpness–generalization premise to develop GEAR-SAM and evaluates its performance. It tests none of V1–V8: its Hessian statistics use the test set, measure unscaled curvature rather than magnitude-aware training-loss perturbation tolerance, and are not compared with training–test gaps. SAM variants with adaptive perturbation allocation are also not tests of V4's adaptive base optimizers.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase captures the authors' overall conclusion: EMA gradient energy guides a constrained block-radius allocation that improves SAM-based optimization and robustness. It should not imply improvement in every condition or equal radii in every experiment: several comparisons favor SAM, and transfer experiments use GEAR-SAM radius 0.2 versus SAM radius 0.05. Budget preservation is a mathematical property relative to a chosen radius; the stabilized implementation realizes perturbation norm at most that radius.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes GEAR-SAM, a SAM variant that allocates the fixed perturbation radius across architecture-level blocks using EMA gradient energy; it does not compare the methods or settings in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Test accuracy varies by dataset, architecture, noise rate, transfer task, and block partition. The reported spectral statistics also differ by training method.

fits_no_version.finding: On ResNet-18/CIFAR-100, test-set Hessian maxima are 365.78, 200.72, and 192.92 for SGD, SAM, and GEAR-SAM. GEAR-SAM's top-50 mean exceeds SAM's, 55.16 versus 52.48.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM-style training changes dominant test-loss curvature; reducing its maximum need not reduce its mean. This does not establish magnitude-aware sharpness tracking generalization gaps.

fits_no_version.finding: GEAR-SAM improves CIFAR-100 accuracy over SAM on all three architectures but is slightly lower on WideResNet/CIFAR-10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Historical block-gradient energy allocation can improve SAM classification performance, with dependence on dataset and architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: GEAR-SAM exceeds SAM at all tested CIFAR-10 noise rates and at CIFAR-100 noise rates of 40–80%, but trails at 20%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: GEAR-SAM can improve noisy-label robustness relative to SAM; this is not evidence of near-perfect random-label fitting.

fits_no_version.finding: GEAR-SAM exceeds SAM in eight of ten transfer conditions, using radius 0.2 versus 0.05.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested GEAR-SAM transfer recipe often improves accuracy over the tested SAM recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: Tensor-wise, coarse, and fine partitions all exceed the SAM accuracy baselines in Table VI.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: GEAR-SAM performance depends on perturbation partition granularity; this does not test widening beyond interpolation.

record.problems: No training-error or train-test-gap results are reported. The Hessian analysis covers ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100 and the text notes that GEAR-SAM does not improve every spectral statistic. Some baseline results are taken directly from prior papers; the paper reports three independent runs and standard deviations for its GEAR-SAM image-classification results.
record.rows_left_out: None; 59 rows retained. The reported test-accuracy and Hessian measurements are not tests of the listed version outcomes, but are kept as results on the claim's generalization and sharpness subject matter.

untested.parts: Joint natural-label generalization, near-perfect fixed-random-label training fit, and chance random-label held-out accuracy under the same recipes.
Width sweeps beyond the zero-training-error threshold and their test-error trajectory.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive base optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning and the stated recovery methods.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove their penalty.
Dropout effects and their dependence on dataset size, strength, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance on training error, association with training–test gaps at similarly low training loss, and ranking against norm and margin measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All rows remain unlinked to V1–V8. Their cannot_determine states concern the listed versions, not whether their reported accuracy differences are readable. Table I baselines are explicitly imported from prior work. No omitted result in the supplied text bears on a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization, natural-label generalization under the same recipes, and random-label held-out performance.
Width sweep across the interpolation threshold and test error beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the effect of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers compared with SGD or momentum under the stated tuning conditions.
Large versus small batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout and its interaction with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight perturbation tolerance and ranking of training-test gaps; the paper measures Hessian eigenvalues, which are not the named measure.
Removal of memorized training examples and the effect on test accuracy.
